Niacinamide Explained: What It Does and Who It Suits

A friendly look at vitamin B3: the benefits research supports, sensible percentages and how to layer it.

By GlowHer Editorial Team · 14 October 2026

Educational content only, not medical advice. Some pages may contain affiliate links. Read our disclosure.

In this article

  1. What it may help with
  2. What percentage should you choose?
  3. How to use it
  4. Possible side effects
  5. Bottom line

Niacinamide is a form of vitamin B3 and one of the most popular and well-studied cosmetic ingredients. It is valued because it is effective, affordable and generally gentle.

What it may help with

  • Supporting the skin barrier and reducing water loss.
  • Making visible pores and shine look more controlled.
  • Evening out the look of skin tone and mild marks.
  • Calming the look of redness for some people.

What percentage should you choose?

Most products sit between 2 and 10 percent. Studies on tone, texture and barrier support commonly use around 2 to 5 percent, and higher numbers are not always better. Start low if your skin is sensitive.

How to use it

Apply after cleansing and before moisturizer, morning or evening. It layers well with hyaluronic acid, ceramides, retinoids and sunscreen.

Possible side effects

Some people notice flushing, tingling or small bumps, especially at higher concentrations or when a formula contains other strong actives. Stop use if you have a reaction and speak with a healthcare professional if it persists.

Bottom line

A niacinamide serum is a sensible first active for oily, combination or uneven-toned skin, and a gentle option for many others.
